Genome-scale charts · Day 02

What We’ll Build Today

Outline · Day 02

From single genes to whole genomes

Yesterday we plotted single experiments and single contrasts. Today we zoom out: the unit of analysis is no longer one gene or one sample, it is the genome itself. Each chart in this deck answers a question that only makes sense at that scale.

  • Stacked bars — composition of mixtures (admixture, microbiome)
  • Time series — trajectories with uncertainty
  • MSA — letters that line up across sequences
  • Manhattan — significance across the whole genome
  • Genome stats — coverage, peaks, gene models
  • pyCirclize — circular genome plots
  • Synteny — comparing genomes side-by-side

Today’s promise Every chart starts from a tidy pandas DataFrame and grows one annotated line at a time. Read the comments — they’re the lesson.

Stacked Bar Plots

Composition · proportions

What Is a Stacked Bar?

Stacked bar · theory

Every column sums to the whole; bands stack to show its parts

A stacked bar answers one question: what is each sample made of? Each column is a single observation (an individual, a tumour, a microbiome sample). The bar is sliced into coloured bands, one per category, and the heights of those bands sum to the total. When every bar has the same total — say, a proportion that must add to 100% — the chart becomes a pure composition view.

Use it when:

  • Admixture / ancestry: each individual = one bar made of ancestry fractions K1…K5.
  • Microbiome: each sample = one bar of phylum or genus relative abundance.
  • Cell-type deconvolution: each tumour = one bar of immune-cell fractions.

Avoid it when only the totals matter (a plain bar chart is clearer) or when you need to compare a single inner band across many samples (segment baselines wobble — a line, dot plot, or small multiples wins).

Anatomy, Before Any Data

Stacked bar · theory

Four bars, five bands — how the geometry works

Before touching real ancestry data, build the idea. Four cartoon bars, each made of five rectangles in the course palette. The trick is the bottom= argument: each band starts where the previous one ended.

Stacked Bar · The Data

Stacked bar · data peek

One row per individual — population label + five ancestry fractions

load_admixture() returns 120 individuals across five reference populations (EUR / EAS / AFR / AMR / SAS). Each row carries five ancestry components K1…K5 whose values sum to 1.0 — they are mixture proportions, the output of a tool like ADMIXTURE or STRUCTURE.

adm = load_admixture()           # individual, population, K1..K5 (K1..K5 sum to 1)
adm.head(5)
individual population K1 K2 K3 K4 K5
0 EUR_000 EUR 0.978699 0.002754 0.000058 0.000306 1.818301e-02
1 EUR_001 EUR 0.978085 0.011594 0.000160 0.001027 9.134997e-03
2 EUR_002 EUR 0.977956 0.009453 0.000056 0.009910 2.624863e-03
3 EUR_003 EUR 0.971030 0.001839 0.025570 0.001560 4.514676e-07
4 EUR_004 EUR 0.945728 0.044775 0.000301 0.000249 8.947892e-03

Stacked Bar · Step 1 — One Individual

Stacked bar · build

1 · A single bar, K1…K5 stacked on top of each other

Build the idea on one person. Take row 0 (an EUR individual), stack their five K fractions vertically with ax.bar(..., bottom=running_total). The bar height ends at exactly 1.0 because the proportions sum.

adm = load_admixture()                          # the full ancestry table
row = adm.iloc[0]                                # one individual (the first EUR)

# the five mixture proportions for this person
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]          # column names in order
fracs  = [row[k] for k in k_cols]                # numeric values, sum to 1.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.8, 4.6))       # CREATE the canvas
bottom = 0                                        # start the stack at y = 0

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                    # one band per K component
    ax.bar(row["individual"], fracs[i],          # CALL: draw this band
           bottom=bottom,                         # stack it atop the previous
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6,
           label=k)
    bottom += fracs[i]                            # next band starts here

ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Stacked Bar · Step 2 — One Population, Sorted

Stacked bar · build

2 · All EUR individuals, sorted by their K1 contribution

Now scale to every EUR individual. Sort them by K1 so the dominant ancestry forms a smooth gradient — without sorting, the bars look like noise. The for loop is unavoidable here: matplotlib’s ax.bar needs the running bottom updated per band.

adm = load_admixture()                                       # full table
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]

eur = adm[adm["population"] == "EUR"].copy()                 # one population
eur = eur.sort_values("K1", ascending=False)                 # gradient by K1

x = np.arange(len(eur))                                       # 0, 1, 2, ... one slot per ind
bottom = np.zeros(len(eur))                                   # running total per bar

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))                    # CREATE the canvas

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                                # one band across all bars
    heights = eur[k].values                                   # bracket access — safe
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,                         # CALL: draw the band
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0,                    # width=1.0: bars touch
           edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights                                          # advance the stack

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(eur) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.set_title("EUR individuals — sorted by K1", color=MUTED, fontsize=11)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Stacked Bar · Step 3 — Every Population

Stacked bar · build

3 · All five populations, separators between groups

The canonical admixture plot. Sort within each population by its dominant K, concatenate, then draw thin vertical lines between groups so the eye can find the boundaries.

adm = load_admixture()                                            # full table
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]                        # fixed order
dom  = {"EUR": "K1", "EAS": "K2", "AFR": "K3", "AMR": "K4", "SAS": "K5"}

# sort each population internally by its dominant K, then concatenate
ordered = pd.concat([
    adm[adm["population"] == p]                                    # one population
       .sort_values(dom[p], ascending=False)                       # gradient inside
    for p in pops
], ignore_index=True)

x = np.arange(len(ordered))                                        # slot per individual
bottom = np.zeros(len(ordered))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 4.2))                         # CREATE the canvas

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                                     # paint each band
    heights = ordered[k].values
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,                              # CALL
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0, edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights

# population boundaries: vertical hairlines
counts = ordered["population"].value_counts().reindex(pops)        # how many per pop
boundaries = counts.cumsum().values[:-1]                            # cut points
for b in boundaries:
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=CREAM, lw=1.5)                       # thin cream divider

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(ordered) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Stacked Bar · Step 4 — Labels & Legend

Stacked bar · build

4 · Population names along the x, K legend on the right

The composition is right; now make it readable. Centre each population’s name under its block of bars using the cumulative counts, and pin the K legend outside the axes so it never overlaps the data.

adm = load_admixture()
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]
dom  = {"EUR": "K1", "EAS": "K2", "AFR": "K3", "AMR": "K4", "SAS": "K5"}

ordered = pd.concat([
    adm[adm["population"] == p].sort_values(dom[p], ascending=False)
    for p in pops
], ignore_index=True)

x = np.arange(len(ordered))
bottom = np.zeros(len(ordered))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 4.4))

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):
    heights = ordered[k].values
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0, edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights

counts = ordered["population"].value_counts().reindex(pops)
boundaries = counts.cumsum().values[:-1]
for b in boundaries:
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=CREAM, lw=1.5)

# population labels: place each at the middle of its block
edges  = np.concatenate([[0], counts.cumsum().values])               # block edges
mids   = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2                                # midpoints
ax.set_xticks(mids)                                                   # tick at each mid
ax.set_xticklabels(pops, color=MUTED, fontsize=10)                    # population names
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0)                                    # hide tick marks

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(ordered) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.set_title("ADMIXTURE K=5 — 120 individuals across 5 populations", color=INK)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(title="component", loc="center left",
          bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Stacked Bar · Pandas Variant

Stacked bar · ergonomic

Three lines with pandas.DataFrame.plot(stacked=True)

Pandas wraps matplotlib for the common case. Set the population-ordered index on the K columns and ask for a stacked bar — pandas computes the running bottom= for you. You give up control (no per-population sort across groups, harder custom separators), but you get to a publishable draft in three lines.

adm = load_admixture()
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]

# group-ordered frame: each pop sorted by its dominant K, indexed by individual
ordered = pd.concat([adm[adm["population"] == p].sort_values(k_cols[i], ascending=False)
                     for i, p in enumerate(pops)], ignore_index=True)
data = ordered.set_index("individual")[k_cols]                # rows=ind, cols=K1..K5

# CALL: pandas builds the whole stacked bar from the frame
ax = data.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, width=1.0,
               color=COURSE_PAL, figsize=(9.0, 4.0), legend=True)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Trade-off: pandas wins on conciseness; matplotlib wins on control — custom separators, per-population sort orders, labels at block midpoints. Use pandas to draft, matplotlib to publish.

Stacked Bar · Takeaway

Stacked bar · recap

Composition first, totals only if they vary

The recipe 1. Each column is one observation; bands stack to its total. 2. Sort within groups by the dominant component — un-sorted admixture looks like noise. 3. One colour per band, fixed across bars — the eye tracks a band by its colour. 4. Separators between groups (thin cream lines) replace heavy x-ticks.

When the totals are forced equal (admixture proportions sum to 1), the stacked bar is pure composition. When totals vary (read counts, dollars), it shows composition and magnitude in one chart. Pick deliberately.

Time Series Plots

Trajectories with uncertainty

What Is a Time Series Plot?

Time series · theory

x is time, y is the measurement, lines show trends, bars or bands show uncertainty

A time series plot answers two questions at once: what is the trajectory, and how confident are we at each point. The x-axis carries time (minutes, hours, days, weeks), the y-axis carries the measurement (expression, abundance, signal). One line per entity traces its trajectory — gene, sample, cell line, patient.

The interesting question is always how to show uncertainty around each point:

  • Error bars (ax.errorbar): vertical whiskers ± SEM or 95% CI at every measured time. Best when you have few points (≤ 6 timepoints) — the eye can read each whisker.
  • Ribbons (ax.fill_between): a translucent band between mean ± SEM. Best when you have many points (a dense kinetic curve) — error bars would clutter; a ribbon shows the envelope at a glance.
  • Small multiples: one panel per entity, faint grey context behind each focal trajectory. Best when you have many entities and lines overlap.

The rule is: pick the encoding that lets the audience read direction + confidence without effort.

Time Series · The Data

Time series · data peek

One row per (gene, timepoint) — tpm with its standard error

load_timecourse() returns a tidy long-form table: 6 genes (BRCA1, TP53, EGFR, MYC, KRAS, PTEN) measured at 5 timepoints (0, 2, 6, 12, 24 hours), with the mean tpm and its standard error sem. Long-form is the format every plotting library expects.

tc = load_timecourse()           # gene, time, tpm, sem  (long-form, 6 genes x 5 timepoints)
tc.head(6)
gene time tpm sem
0 BRCA1 0 13.0 3.062475
1 BRCA1 2 15.0 1.901278
2 BRCA1 6 17.0 2.320425
3 BRCA1 12 17.0 2.690532
4 BRCA1 24 23.0 3.510216
5 TP53 0 23.0 3.334770

Time Series · The .sem Footgun

Time series · gotcha

DataFrame.sem is a method. Always use bracket access for the column

This dataset has a column literally called sem — the standard error of the mean. But pandas DataFrames already have a .sem() method (it computes the standard error). Dot access loses to the method every time and you get a confusing error. The fix is one character: brackets.

The bug — tc.sem returns the method, not the column:

tc = load_timecourse()

tc.sem                       # bound method, not data
# <bound method ... DataFrame.sem of ...>

tc.sem.values                # AttributeError!
# AttributeError: 'function' object
#  has no attribute 'values'

When you pass yerr=tc.sem to matplotlib you get a cryptic TypeError because matplotlib tried to use the method as an array.

The fix — always use bracket access:

tc = load_timecourse()

tc["sem"]                    # the actual column
# 0    3.062
# 1    1.901
# ...

tc["sem"].values             # plain numpy array
# array([3.06, 1.90, 2.32, ...])

Rule of thumb: prefer df["col"] over df.col always. Brackets work for every legal name; dots silently break on mean, sum, sem, count, index, T, …

Time Series · Step 1 — One Gene

Time series · build

1 · BRCA1 only, time vs tpm

Build the idea on one gene. Filter the long table to BRCA1, draw time on x and tpm on y. A single ax.plot with markers tells the trajectory.

tc = load_timecourse()                              # the full long-form table
brca1 = tc[tc["gene"] == "BRCA1"]                   # filter to one gene

# sanity check: 5 rows, one per timepoint
brca1 = brca1.sort_values("time")                   # ensure x is monotonic

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.2))          # CREATE the canvas
ax.plot(brca1["time"], brca1["tpm"],                # CALL: x = time, y = tpm
        marker="o", color=COURSE_PAL[0], lw=2,      # green-teal "story" line
        markersize=6)

ax.set_xlabel("time (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("tpm")
ax.set_title("BRCA1 expression over 24h", color=INK)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Time Series · Step 2 — All Six Genes

Time series · build

2 · One line per gene, distinct on-palette colours

Loop the six genes and draw one line per gene. The course palette covers five; for the sixth we use a neutral grey — a deliberate de-emphasis, the gene that doesn’t compete for attention.

tc = load_timecourse()                                       # full long-form table
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS", "PTEN"]     # fixed order

# six colours: five course-palette + one neutral GREY for the last
palette = COURSE_PAL + [GREY]                                 # length-6 colour list

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.4))                    # CREATE the canvas

for gene, colour in zip(genes, palette):                      # one line per gene
    g = tc[tc["gene"] == gene].sort_values("time")            # filter + order
    ax.plot(g["time"], g["tpm"],                              # CALL: trajectory
            marker="o", color=colour, lw=2,
            markersize=5, label=gene)

ax.set_xlabel("time (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("tpm")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
          frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Time Series · Step 3 — Error Bars

Time series · build

3 · ax.errorbar adds vertical whiskers at every point

Swap ax.plot for ax.errorbar and pass yerr=g["sem"]. The capsize=3 gives the little horizontal caps that make whiskers readable. Bracket access is mandatory — g.sem is the method (slide 17).

tc = load_timecourse()
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS", "PTEN"]
palette = COURSE_PAL + [GREY]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.4))

for gene, colour in zip(genes, palette):
    g = tc[tc["gene"] == gene].sort_values("time")

    # CALL: line + whiskers in one call. yerr=g["sem"], NOT g.sem
    ax.errorbar(g["time"], g["tpm"],
                yerr=g["sem"],                       # bracket access — sem is a column
                marker="o", color=colour, lw=2,
                markersize=5,
                capsize=3,                            # caps make whiskers readable
                label=gene)

ax.set_xlabel("time (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("tpm  (mean ± SEM)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
          frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Time Series · Step 4 — Ribbons

Time series · build

4 · ax.fill_between replaces whiskers with a translucent envelope

When lines are dense, whiskers stack and clutter. Swap them for a ribbon: ax.fill_between(time, tpm − sem, tpm + sem, alpha=0.25). The trajectory stays sharp; the uncertainty becomes a soft halo around it.

tc = load_timecourse()
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS", "PTEN"]
palette = COURSE_PAL + [GREY]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.4))

for gene, colour in zip(genes, palette):
    g = tc[tc["gene"] == gene].sort_values("time")

    # CALL 1: the trajectory line, sharp on top
    ax.plot(g["time"], g["tpm"],
            color=colour, lw=2, marker="o", markersize=5, label=gene)

    # CALL 2: the uncertainty ribbon, translucent below
    ax.fill_between(g["time"],
                    g["tpm"] - g["sem"],             # lower edge of the band
                    g["tpm"] + g["sem"],             # upper edge of the band
                    color=colour, alpha=0.20,        # see-through halo
                    linewidth=0)

ax.set_xlabel("time (hours)")
ax.set_ylabel("tpm  (mean ± SEM)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
          frameon=False, fontsize=9)

Time Series · Step 5 — Small Multiples

Time series · build

5 · One panel per gene, faint grey context behind each focal trajectory

The killer plot. A 2×3 grid, one gene per panel in its colour with its SEM ribbon, and every other gene drawn faintly in grey behind it so each panel has full context. sharex=True, sharey=True keeps the axes comparable across panels.

tc = load_timecourse()
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS", "PTEN"]
palette = COURSE_PAL + [GREY]

# CREATE: 2 rows x 3 cols, shared axes for easy across-panel comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(8.4, 4.8),
                          sharex=True, sharey=True)
axes = axes.flatten()                                          # 6 axes, easy indexing

for ax, gene, colour in zip(axes, genes, palette):
    # context: every other gene as a faint grey line behind
    for other in genes:
        if other == gene:                                       # skip the focal
            continue
        o = tc[tc["gene"] == other].sort_values("time")
        ax.plot(o["time"], o["tpm"],
                color=LINE, lw=1, alpha=0.6, zorder=1)         # de-emphasised context

    # focal gene: full colour, ribbon, marker
    g = tc[tc["gene"] == gene].sort_values("time")
    ax.plot(g["time"], g["tpm"], color=colour, lw=2.2,
            marker="o", markersize=4, zorder=3)                # on top of context
    ax.fill_between(g["time"], g["tpm"] - g["sem"], g["tpm"] + g["sem"],
                    color=colour, alpha=0.22, linewidth=0, zorder=2)

    ax.set_title(gene, color=colour, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.supxlabel("time (hours)"); fig.supylabel("tpm")
plt.tight_layout()

Time Series · Seaborn Variant

Time series · ergonomic

One sns.lineplot call replaces the loop

Seaborn understands long-form data natively. Pass the whole tc table, name the columns, and use hue="gene" — seaborn does the per-gene split, the colour cycling, and the standard-error ribbon (errorbar="se") in one call. The cost: less control over each line’s styling.

tc = load_timecourse()

# CALL: one line per `gene`, ribbon from `errorbar="se"`
ax = sns.lineplot(
    data=tc, x="time", y="tpm",
    hue="gene",                                       # split by gene -> 6 colours
    hue_order=["BRCA1","TP53","EGFR","MYC","KRAS","PTEN"],
    palette=COURSE_PAL + [GREY],                      # the same 6-colour list
    errorbar="se",                                    # ribbon = ± standard error
    marker="o", linewidth=2)

ax.set_xlabel("time (hours)"); ax.set_ylabel("tpm")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
          frameon=False, fontsize=9, title="")

Trade-off: seaborn collapses the loop and adds a ribbon for free — perfect for exploration. matplotlib’s explicit loop wins when you need bespoke styling per line (one bold, the rest dimmed; mixed dashes; small-multiples). Use seaborn to see, matplotlib to publish.

Time Series · Takeaway

Time series · recap

Trajectory plus uncertainty, scaled to your data

The recipe 1. Lines tell direction, error bars or ribbons tell confidence. 2. Error bars for few points (≤ 6 timepoints); ribbons for many. 3. Small multiples isolate each story when lines overlap — keep faint grey context behind each panel. 4. Always use bracket access for df["sem"] — the dot-attribute collides with DataFrame.sem() and silently breaks.

Direction + confidence + isolation: the three knobs of every time-series figure. Pick the one your audience needs most for this plot.

Multiple Sequence Alignment

Comparative sequences

What Is an MSA?

MSA · theory

N sequences, one column at a time

A multiple sequence alignment (MSA) stacks N related sequences so that homologous positions sit in the same column. Reading top-to-bottom in one column tells you how that letter varies across species, samples, or strains. Reading left-to-right is one full sequence.

Three things the eye looks for:

  • Conserved columns — every row carries the same letter. These mark functionally important sites (active-site residues, splice motifs, transcription-factor footprints).
  • Gap columns (-) — an insertion in one lineage or a deletion in another. Gaps interrupt the grid like vertical white stripes.
  • Mismatched columns — divergence. Useful for phylogenetic distance, but only after the alignment is trustworthy.

Colour encodes chemistry: the Clustal scheme groups hydrophobic, polar, acidic, and basic residues so families pop. For DNA we just colour by identity (A, C, G, T) — four hues is enough.

When to use it: phylogeny, conserved-domain hunting, primer design, regulatory motif discovery, variant interpretation.

MSA · The Data

MSA · data peek

Synthesise 8 sequences × 60 columns, low mutation rate + one indel

No real loader: we build a toy alignment in numpy. Start from one random ACGT base sequence, derive seven mutants with ~5 % per-base substitutions, then punch a small deletion (-) into one sequence at columns 22–26. That gives a realistic-looking conservation pattern with one obvious gap.

# 60-column base sequence drawn uniformly from ACGT
n_cols = 60                                                 # alignment width
n_rows = 8                                                  # number of sequences
bases  = np.array(list("ACGT"))                             # the alphabet

# seq 0 is the ancestor; seqs 1..7 inherit then mutate
base = rng.choice(bases, size=n_cols)                       # one random ACGT row
aln  = np.tile(base, (n_rows, 1))                           # 8 identical copies

# at each position in each non-ancestor row, mutate with p ≈ 5 %
mutate = rng.random((n_rows, n_cols)) < 0.05                # boolean mask
mutate[0] = False                                           # row 0 stays as ancestor
aln[mutate] = rng.choice(bases, size=mutate.sum())          # swap in a new base

# introduce a clean 5-column deletion in sequence 5 (cols 22..26)
aln[5, 22:27] = "-"                                         # the indel block

print(aln.shape)                                            # (8, 60)
print("\n".join("".join(row) for row in aln))               # show the alignment text
(8, 60)
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTTGTCAGCGTCTACTAGCGTTTGTTAACGTCTCTGGAGTTTTA
AATCGGGACACTGAGTTTTGTCAGCGTCTATTAGCGTTTGTTAACGTCTCTGAAGTTTTA
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTTGTCAGCGTCTACTAGCGTTTGTTAACGTCTCTGGAGTTTTA
AATCGTGACACTGAGATTTGTCAGCGTCTACTAGCCGTTGTTAACGTCTCTGGAGTTTTA
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTAGTCAGCGTCTAGTACCGTTTGGTAACGTGTCTGGAGTTTTT
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTAGTC-----TTACTAGCGTTTGTTAACGTCTCTGGAGTTTTA
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTTGTCAGCGTCTACTAGCGTTTGTTAACGTCTCTGGAGTTTTA
AATCGGGACACTGAGATTTGTCAGCGTCTACTAGCGTGTGTTAACGTCTCTGAAGTTTTA

MSA · Step 1 — Coloured Letter Grid

MSA · build

1 · Draw each base as text at (col, row)

The simplest renderer: walk the array and place every letter with ax.text(col, row, letter, color=...). Matplotlib uses data coordinates, so (col, row) puts column 0 at the left edge and row 0 at the top — but matplotlib’s y-axis grows upward by default, so we invert the y-axis to read top-to-bottom like a text file.

# rebuild the alignment so the slide is self-contained
n_cols, n_rows = 60, 8                                  # alignment shape
bases = np.array(list("ACGT"))                          # DNA alphabet

base = rng.choice(bases, size=n_cols)                   # ancestor row
aln = np.tile(base, (n_rows, 1))                        # 8 copies
mutate = rng.random((n_rows, n_cols)) < 0.05            # 5 % mutation mask
mutate[0] = False                                       # keep ancestor clean
aln[mutate] = rng.choice(bases, size=mutate.sum())      # apply mutations
aln[5, 22:27] = "-"                                     # one indel block

# colour by base identity — Economist palette, GREY for gaps
col_map = {"A": GREEN, "C": BLUE, "G": AMBER, "T": RED, "-": GREY}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 2.6))              # CREATE wide canvas
for r in range(n_rows):                                 # one row of sequence
    for c in range(n_cols):                             # one column position
        letter = aln[r, c]                              # the base at (r, c)
        ax.text(c, r, letter, ha="center", va="center", # CALL: draw letter
                color=col_map[letter], fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, n_cols - 0.5)                         # column range
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, n_rows - 0.5)                         # row range
ax.invert_yaxis()                                       # row 0 at the top
ax.set_yticks(range(n_rows))                            # one tick per sequence
ax.set_yticklabels([f"seq{r}" for r in range(n_rows)])  # sequence labels
ax.set_xticks([])                                       # column ticks add noise
ax.spines[["top", "right", "bottom"]].set_visible(False)

MSA · Step 2 — Heatmap Encoding

MSA · build

2 · Paint cells, overlay letters in white

The letter-grid is friendly but doesn’t scale past ~30 rows. Replace it with a coloured heatmap: encode each base as an integer (A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3, -=4), feed that to ax.imshow with a ListedColormap of the five palette colours, then overlay each letter in white on top. The same picture, now scalable to hundreds of sequences.

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

# rebuild alignment
n_cols, n_rows = 60, 8
bases = np.array(list("ACGT"))
base = rng.choice(bases, size=n_cols); aln = np.tile(base, (n_rows, 1))
mutate = rng.random((n_rows, n_cols)) < 0.05; mutate[0] = False
aln[mutate] = rng.choice(bases, size=mutate.sum()); aln[5, 22:27] = "-"

# encode each letter as an integer in [0..4]
code = {"A": 0, "C": 1, "G": 2, "T": 3, "-": 4}         # letter -> index
aln_int = np.vectorize(code.get)(aln)                   # int array, same shape
cmap = ListedColormap([GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, "#FFFFFF"])  # one colour per code

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 2.6))              # CREATE canvas
ax.imshow(aln_int, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto",            # CALL: paint cells
          interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=4)

# overlay each letter in white so the identity is still legible
for r in range(n_rows):
    for c in range(n_cols):
        letter = aln[r, c]
        if letter != "-":                               # skip gaps (white cell)
            ax.text(c, r, letter, ha="center", va="center",
                    color="white", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_yticks(range(n_rows))                            # sequence labels
ax.set_yticklabels([f"seq{r}" for r in range(n_rows)])
ax.set_xticks([])                                       # hide column ticks
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

MSA · Step 3 — Conservation Track

MSA · build

3 · Bar above the grid, one bar per column

The canonical MSA viewer layout is two stacked panels sharing the x-axis: a tall bottom panel with the alignment, a short top panel with a conservation bar per column. Compute conservation as the fraction of rows showing the most-common non-gap base — 1.0 means every sequence agrees, 0.25 means random.

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

n_cols, n_rows = 60, 8
bases = np.array(list("ACGT"))
base = rng.choice(bases, size=n_cols); aln = np.tile(base, (n_rows, 1))
mutate = rng.random((n_rows, n_cols)) < 0.05; mutate[0] = False
aln[mutate] = rng.choice(bases, size=mutate.sum()); aln[5, 22:27] = "-"

# conservation = fraction of most-common non-gap letter per column
def col_conservation(col):
    non_gap = col[col != "-"]                           # drop gaps before counting
    if len(non_gap) == 0:                               # all-gap column edge case
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(non_gap, return_counts=True)  # tally each base
    return counts.max() / len(non_gap)                  # majority fraction
conservation = np.array([col_conservation(aln[:, c]) for c in range(n_cols)])

# CREATE two stacked panels — short bar track on top, alignment below
fig, (axc, axa) = plt.subplots(                         # axc = conservation, axa = aln
    2, 1, figsize=(9.5, 3.4), sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 4], hspace=0.05))

axc.bar(np.arange(n_cols), conservation,                # CALL: per-column bars
        color=GREEN, width=0.9)
axc.set_ylim(0, 1.05); axc.set_yticks([0, 1])
axc.set_ylabel("cons.", fontsize=8)
axc.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# the alignment heatmap, identical to step 2
code = {"A": 0, "C": 1, "G": 2, "T": 3, "-": 4}
aln_int = np.vectorize(code.get)(aln)
cmap = ListedColormap([GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, "#FFFFFF"])
axa.imshow(aln_int, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=4)
axa.set_yticks(range(n_rows)); axa.set_yticklabels([f"seq{r}" for r in range(n_rows)])
axa.set_xlabel("column"); axa.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

MSA · Step 4 — Zoom to the Indel

MSA · build

4 · Crop to columns 20–30; the gap is the story

At full width every column is one pixel wide and the eye washes out. Zoom with ax.set_xlim(20, 30) to the indel region — now the gap block (cols 22–26 in seq5) reads as five empty cells, and the surrounding conservation is clear column by column. Working MSAs always combine an overview with a zoom.

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

n_cols, n_rows = 60, 8
bases = np.array(list("ACGT"))
base = rng.choice(bases, size=n_cols); aln = np.tile(base, (n_rows, 1))
mutate = rng.random((n_rows, n_cols)) < 0.05; mutate[0] = False
aln[mutate] = rng.choice(bases, size=mutate.sum()); aln[5, 22:27] = "-"

def col_conservation(col):
    non_gap = col[col != "-"]
    if len(non_gap) == 0: return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(non_gap, return_counts=True)
    return counts.max() / len(non_gap)
conservation = np.array([col_conservation(aln[:, c]) for c in range(n_cols)])

fig, (axc, axa) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(8.5, 3.6), sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 4], hspace=0.05))

axc.bar(np.arange(n_cols), conservation, color=GREEN, width=0.9)
axc.set_ylim(0, 1.05); axc.set_yticks([0, 1])
axc.set_ylabel("cons.", fontsize=8)
axc.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

code = {"A": 0, "C": 1, "G": 2, "T": 3, "-": 4}
aln_int = np.vectorize(code.get)(aln)
cmap = ListedColormap([GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, "#FFFFFF"])
axa.imshow(aln_int, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=4)
for r in range(n_rows):                                 # letters are legible at this zoom
    for c in range(20, 31):
        letter = aln[r, c]
        if letter != "-":
            axa.text(c, r, letter, ha="center", va="center",
                     color="white", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

# crop both panels to the indel neighbourhood
axa.set_xlim(19.5, 30.5)                                # zoom x-axis
axa.set_xticks(range(20, 31))                           # one tick per column
axa.set_yticks(range(n_rows)); axa.set_yticklabels([f"seq{r}" for r in range(n_rows)])
axa.set_xlabel("column"); axa.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

MSA · Production Tools

MSA · ecosystem

Biopython for I/O, pyMSAviz for paper-ready output

For real work, don’t roll your own — two libraries cover it:

Biopython reads/writes every common alignment format (FASTA, Clustal, Stockholm, PHYLIP) and gives you a numpy-like view:

from Bio import AlignIO
aln = AlignIO.read("globins.aln", "clustal")
for record in aln:
    print(record.id, record.seq[:60])

pyMSAviz renders Clustal-coloured, paper-ready figures with conservation tracks, consensus rows, and reasonable defaults:

from pymsaviz import MsaViz
mv = MsaViz("globins.aln", color_scheme="Clustal",
            wrap_length=60, show_consensus=True)
mv.savefig("globins_msa.png")

The matplotlib build you just saw is the mental model; these libraries do the same thing with more polish and more formats.

MSA · Takeaway

MSA · recap

What the eye is reading

The recipe 1. Conservation, identity, gaps — three things the reader scans for in every column. 2. Colour encodes chemistry (Clustal) or identity (A/C/G/T). Four-to-five hues is enough; gaps are grey or white. 3. Conservation track on top of the heatmap turns the eye to interesting columns automatically. 4. Always zoom. A full-width MSA is a dense mosaic; the story lives in a 10–20 column window.

Manhattan Plots

GWAS · genome-wide significance

What Is a Manhattan Plot?

Manhattan · theory

One dot per SNP, the whole genome on the x-axis

A Manhattan plot is the canonical view of a genome-wide association study (GWAS). Each dot is one variant. The x-axis is genomic position — every chromosome laid end-to-end — and the y-axis is the −log10 of the association p-value. So higher = stronger evidence that the variant is linked to the trait.

The shape that gives it its name: most SNPs are background noise, a flat low cloud — but real signals rise into thin skyscrapers that look like the New York skyline. The eye reads “significance peaks above the horizon line”.

Two horizontal cutoffs:

  • Suggestive line: p = 1e-5 (often shown as -log10(p) = 5)
  • Genome-wide significance line: p = 5e-8 (-log10(p) ≈ 7.3) — the canonical Bonferroni-corrected threshold for ~1 M independent tests in the human genome.

Anatomy, Before Any Data

Manhattan · theory

Three regions before we even load a file

Manhattan · The Data

Manhattan · data peek

One row per SNP — chrom, pos, p-value, rsID

load_gwas("height") returns a tidy table: 13 475 SNPs across 22 chromosomes, with raw p-values. The simulation seeds a few real-looking peaks so the build has something to point at.

gwas = load_gwas("height")        # chrom, pos, pval, snp
gwas.head(5)
chrom pos pval snp
0 1 562879 0.197842 rs1217797
1 1 802716 0.454291 rs3152883
2 1 933561 0.750287 rs1966161
3 1 1294717 0.707315 rs2836508
4 1 1316327 0.553459 rs6514392

Manhattan · Step 1 — One Chromosome First

Manhattan · build

1 · The cloud, on chromosome 1 only

Before we tile 22 chromosomes, build the idea on one. Scatter SNP position vs −log10(p). The shape is already there: a flat cloud with the occasional spike.

gwas = load_gwas("height")                       # the whole-genome table

chr1 = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == 1].copy()           # one chromosome only
chr1["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(chr1["pval"])        # significance axis

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))           # CREATE the canvas
ax.scatter(chr1["pos"], chr1["nlog10p"],         # CALL: x = bp, y = -log10(p)
           s=8, color=GREY, alpha=0.5, linewidths=0)

ax.set_xlabel("position on chr1 (bp)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$-\log_{10}(p)$")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Manhattan · Step 2 — All 22, Alternating Colours

Manhattan · build

2 · Lay every chromosome end-to-end

The trick: replace per-chromosome pos with a cumulative coordinate so chr2 starts where chr1 ends. Alternate two colours so the eye can tell chromosomes apart without a heavy x-axis.

gwas = load_gwas("height").sort_values(["chrom", "pos"]).copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])

# 1. find each chromosome's length, then offset cumulatively
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max()
offsets = chrom_len.cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)        # chr1→0, chr2→len(chr1), ...
gwas["cum_pos"] = gwas["pos"] + gwas["chrom"].map(offsets)

# 2. one colour per parity (Economist BLUE / GREEN), painless cycler
palette = {True: BLUE, False: GREEN}
gwas["color"] = (gwas["chrom"] % 2 == 0).map(palette)

# 3. scatter once with the precomputed colour column
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4))
ax.scatter(gwas["cum_pos"], gwas["nlog10p"],
           c=gwas["color"], s=6, alpha=0.7, linewidths=0)

# 4. x-ticks at each chromosome's mid-point, not every megabase
tick_pos = offsets + chrom_len / 2
ax.set_xticks(tick_pos); ax.set_xticklabels(chrom_len.index, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("chromosome"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$-\log_{10}(p)$")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Manhattan · Step 3 — The Significance Lines

Manhattan · build

3 · Draw the thresholds the field agrees on

Two dashed horizontals turn the cloud into a test: suggestive (p = 1e-5) and genome-wide (p = 5e-8). Anything above the upper line is the headline of the paper.

gwas = load_gwas("height").sort_values(["chrom", "pos"]).copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])

chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max()
offsets = chrom_len.cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)
gwas["cum_pos"] = gwas["pos"] + gwas["chrom"].map(offsets)

palette = {True: BLUE, False: GREEN}
gwas["color"] = (gwas["chrom"] % 2 == 0).map(palette)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4))
ax.scatter(gwas["cum_pos"], gwas["nlog10p"],
           c=gwas["color"], s=6, alpha=0.7, linewidths=0)

tick_pos = offsets + chrom_len / 2
ax.set_xticks(tick_pos); ax.set_xticklabels(chrom_len.index, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("chromosome"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$-\log_{10}(p)$")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# 5. the thresholds — dashed, annotated on the right edge
ax.axhline(-np.log10(5e-8), color=RED,   lw=.9, ls="--")   # genome-wide
ax.axhline(-np.log10(1e-5), color=AMBER, lw=.9, ls="--")   # suggestive
ax.text(gwas["cum_pos"].max(), -np.log10(5e-8)+0.15, "p = 5e-8",
        ha="right", va="bottom", color=RED,   fontsize=8)
ax.text(gwas["cum_pos"].max(), -np.log10(1e-5)+0.15, "p = 1e-5",
        ha="right", va="bottom", color=AMBER, fontsize=8)

Manhattan · Step 4 — Highlight & Label the Hits

Manhattan · build

4 · Spotlight the SNPs that crossed the line

Genome-wide significant hits get a filled red dot on top of the cloud and an rsID label. The audience finally sees what the paper claims.

gwas = load_gwas("height").sort_values(["chrom", "pos"]).copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])

chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max()
offsets = chrom_len.cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)
gwas["cum_pos"] = gwas["pos"] + gwas["chrom"].map(offsets)

palette = {True: BLUE, False: GREEN}
gwas["color"] = (gwas["chrom"] % 2 == 0).map(palette)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.3))
ax.scatter(gwas["cum_pos"], gwas["nlog10p"],
           c=gwas["color"], s=6, alpha=0.55, linewidths=0)

ax.axhline(-np.log10(5e-8), color=RED,   lw=.9, ls="--")
ax.axhline(-np.log10(1e-5), color=AMBER, lw=.9, ls="--")

tick_pos = offsets + chrom_len / 2
ax.set_xticks(tick_pos); ax.set_xticklabels(chrom_len.index, fontsize=8)

# 6. spotlight — the hits as bigger red dots, on top (high zorder)
hits = gwas[gwas["pval"] < 5e-8]
ax.scatter(hits["cum_pos"], hits["nlog10p"],
           color=RED, s=42, edgecolor="white", linewidths=0.6, zorder=5)

# 7. label the top 3 by significance with their rsIDs
for _, row in hits.nsmallest(3, "pval").iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row["snp"], (row["cum_pos"], row["nlog10p"]),
                xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)

ax.set_xlabel("chromosome")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$-\log_{10}(p)$")
ax.set_title(f"Height GWAS — {len(hits)} genome-wide significant SNPs")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Manhattan · Plotly Variant

Manhattan · interactive

Hover for the SNP ID — same plot, browser-native interactivity

For dashboards and exploratory review, plotly gives every dot a tooltip. Same logic as the matplotlib version — cumulative x, parity colour, threshold line — but hover_data exposes chrom / pos / rsID.

import plotly.express as px

# reuse the prepared frame (cum_pos, nlog10p, color)
gwas = load_gwas("height").sort_values(["chrom", "pos"]).copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max()
offsets = chrom_len.cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)
gwas["cum_pos"] = gwas["pos"] + gwas["chrom"].map(offsets)
gwas["chrom_parity"] = (gwas["chrom"] % 2 == 0).astype(str)

# px.scatter handles colour grouping + hover for us
fig = px.scatter(
    gwas, x="cum_pos", y="nlog10p",
    color="chrom_parity",
    color_discrete_map={"True": BLUE, "False": GREEN},
    hover_data=["chrom", "pos", "snp", "pval"],
    labels={"cum_pos": "genomic position", "nlog10p": "-log10(p)"})

fig.add_hline(y=-np.log10(5e-8), line_dash="dash", line_color=RED)
fig.add_hline(y=-np.log10(1e-5), line_dash="dash", line_color=AMBER)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=4, opacity=0.6))
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, height=420,
                  paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM)
fig

Manhattan · Takeaway

Manhattan · recap

Four ideas, every time

The recipe 1. Cumulative position so chromosomes lay end-to-end. 2. Two-colour parity so neighbours are visually separable without ticks. 3. Two threshold lines — suggestive (1e-5) and genome-wide (5e-8). 4. Highlight + label the hits; the cloud is context, the spikes are the story.

The same four ideas drive most genome-scale dot plots: methylation Manhattans, peak-significance plots, mutation rate scans. Once you’ve built one, you’ve built them all.

Genome Statistics

Coverage · peaks · gene models

Three Questions, Three Charts

Genome stats · theory

What is the chart actually answering?

Genome-stats figures crowd into papers and dashboards, but each one is really asking one of three questions:

  • Is my sample any good? Coverage and callable-fraction QC: per-sample bar charts, dumbbells, ridge plots. The chart fails if the reader can’t spot the dropouts at a glance.
  • Where in the genome is the signal? Peak tracks for ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, methylation. The x-axis is genomic coordinate; the y-axis is signal height. Multiple marks stack vertically with a shared x-axis.
  • What gene is there? A gene-model track of rectangles with strand-aware arrowheads, drawn under the signal panels so the reader can connect a peak to a feature.

A paper-ready ChIP-seq screenshot is just these three answers, stacked, sharing one x-axis. We’ll build it.

Genome Stats · The QC Data

Coverage · data peek

One row per sample — raw vs callable rate, with the loss

load_qc() is twelve sequencing libraries with two metrics:

  • raw — fraction of reads that map at all (alignment rate).
  • callable — fraction of reads that survive duplicate removal, MAPQ filtering, and duplicate-clipping (the bases you can actually call variants from).
  • loss — raw − callable. Large loss = a problem sample: high duplication, contamination, or PCR over-amplification.
qc = load_qc()                       # sample, raw, callable, loss
qc.head(6)
sample raw callable loss
0 S01 92.7 88.2 4.5
1 S02 94.1 68.1 26.0
2 S03 92.7 88.1 4.6
3 S04 95.0 92.9 2.1
4 S05 93.7 89.2 4.5
5 S06 93.4 89.3 4.1

Coverage · Step 1 — One Sample, Two Bars

Coverage · build

1 · The simplest possible view

Start with a single sample to fix the colour grammar: GREEN for raw (what mapped), AMBER for callable (what survived filters). Side-by-side bars make the gap visible.

qc = load_qc()                                          # 12 samples
one = qc.iloc[0]                                        # the first sample

vals   = [one["raw"], one["callable"]]                  # two heights
labels = ["raw", "callable"]                            # two bar names
colors = [GREEN, AMBER]                                 # palette grammar

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.4, 4.2))              # CREATE compact canvas
ax.bar(labels, vals, color=colors, width=0.6)           # CALL: side-by-side bars

# annotate each bar with its percentage so the gap is unambiguous
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.01, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom",
            color=INK, fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)

ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)                                    # fraction axis
ax.set_ylabel("fraction of reads")
ax.set_title(f"{one['sample']} — raw vs callable", color=INK)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Coverage · Step 2 — Dumbbell Across All Samples

Coverage · build

2 · One lane per sample, sorted by loss

Twelve side-by-side bar pairs is noisy. The canonical view is a dumbbell: each sample is one horizontal lane with a thin grey line spanning raw → callable, a GREEN dot at raw, and an AMBER dot at callable. Sort samples by loss (biggest first) and the worst offenders rise to the top.

qc = load_qc().sort_values("loss", ascending=False)     # worst loss on top
qc = qc.reset_index(drop=True)                          # 0..N for the y-axis

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.6))              # CREATE wide-ish canvas

# one thin grey line per sample, from raw down to callable
ax.hlines(y=qc.index, xmin=qc["callable"], xmax=qc["raw"],
          color=LINE, lw=2, zorder=1)                   # the "bar" of the dumbbell

# GREEN dot = where we started (raw); AMBER dot = what survived (callable)
ax.scatter(qc["raw"],      qc.index, color=GREEN, s=80, zorder=3, label="raw")
ax.scatter(qc["callable"], qc.index, color=AMBER, s=80, zorder=3, label="callable")

# y-axis = sample label, top-to-bottom = worst loss to best
ax.set_yticks(qc.index)
ax.set_yticklabels(qc["sample"], fontsize=8)
ax.invert_yaxis()                                       # biggest loss at top
ax.set_xlim(0.4, 1.0)                                   # tighten the lens
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of reads")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=9)

# annotate loss in % at the right edge of each lane
for _, row in qc.iterrows():
    ax.text(row["raw"] + 0.005, row.name, f"-{row['loss']:.0%}",
            va="center", color=MUTED, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Per-sample callable-rate loss", color=INK)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

Genome Stats · The Peak Data

Peaks + genes · data peek

Two tidy tables — signal tracks and gene annotations

load_peaks() is one row per genomic position with three signal columns. load_peak_genes() is one row per gene with start/end/strand.

peaks = load_peaks()                # position, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC
peaks.head(5)
position H3K27ac H3K4me3 ATAC
0 0.00000 0.069866 0.048841 0.000581
1 20.02002 0.053866 0.048752 0.019810
2 40.04004 0.054921 0.019941 0.081723
3 60.06006 0.014632 0.008636 0.053283
4 80.08008 0.093176 0.043320 0.021620 
genes = load_peak_genes()           # name, start, end, strand
genes.head(5)
name start end strand
0 GeneA 1500 4500 +
1 GeneB 7000 10500 -
2 GeneC 13500 17000 +

H3K27ac marks active enhancers, H3K4me3 marks active promoters, ATAC marks open chromatin. Together they triangulate “where is something happening”.

Peaks · Step 3 — Three Stacked Signal Tracks

Peaks · build

3 · One mark per panel, shared x-axis

Three filled-area panels stacked vertically with sharex=True. The shared x-axis is the contract — column-aligned positions across all panels let the eye spot a triple co-occurrence (active promoter + active enhancer + open chromatin) at a single x-coordinate.

peaks = load_peaks()                                    # position + 3 signal cols
x = peaks["position"]                                   # shared genomic axis

# CREATE three panels stacked, all sharing the x-axis
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    3, 1, figsize=(8.8, 4.2), sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.15))
ax_ac, ax_k4, ax_at = axes                              # name each panel

# top panel: H3K27ac — active enhancer mark, RED
ax_ac.fill_between(x, peaks["H3K27ac"], where=peaks["H3K27ac"] > 0,
                   color=RED, alpha=0.7)               # CALL: filled area
ax_ac.set_ylabel("H3K27ac"); ax_ac.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# middle panel: H3K4me3 — active promoter mark, BLUE
ax_k4.fill_between(x, peaks["H3K4me3"], where=peaks["H3K4me3"] > 0,
                   color=BLUE, alpha=0.7)
ax_k4.set_ylabel("H3K4me3"); ax_k4.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# bottom panel: ATAC — open chromatin, GREEN
ax_at.fill_between(x, peaks["ATAC"], where=peaks["ATAC"] > 0,
                   color=GREEN, alpha=0.7)
ax_at.set_ylabel("ATAC"); ax_at.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax_at.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")

Peaks · Step 4 — Gene Model on Its Own

Peaks · build

4 · Rectangles for gene bodies, arrowheads for strand

Before we glue it to the signal tracks, get the gene model right on its own axis. Each gene is a Rectangle spanning start → end. Strand is encoded with a small arrowhead — a triangular Polygon pointing right for + strand, left for −.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon

genes = load_peak_genes()                               # name, start, end, strand
peaks = load_peaks()                                    # only used for x range
xmin, xmax = peaks["position"].min(), peaks["position"].max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 1.6))              # CREATE thin track canvas

# helper to draw one gene as body + arrowhead + name
def draw_gene(ax, row):
    y, h = 0, 0.4                                       # vertical centre and height
    body = Rectangle((row["start"], y - h / 2),         # rectangle anchor (x, y)
                     row["end"] - row["start"], h,       # width = gene length
                     facecolor=PURPLE, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.8)
    ax.add_patch(body)                                  # CALL: gene body
    # strand-aware arrowhead at the leading edge of the gene
    if row["strand"] == "+":
        tip_x, base_x = row["end"], row["end"] - 400    # points right
    else:
        tip_x, base_x = row["start"], row["start"] + 400  # points left
    head = Polygon([(base_x, y - h / 2), (base_x, y + h / 2), (tip_x, y)],
                   facecolor=PURPLE, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.8)
    ax.add_patch(head)
    ax.text((row["start"] + row["end"]) / 2, y + 0.45,  # gene name above body
            row["name"], ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")

# draw every gene; peak_genes has only 3
for _, row in genes.iterrows():
    draw_gene(ax, row)

ax.set_xlim(xmin, xmax)                                 # match peak panel range
ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)                                      # one lane, generous headroom
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)  # minimalist frame

Peaks · Step 5 — Four-Panel Paper Figure

Peaks · build

5 · Three signal panels + one gene model, one shared x-axis

Glue everything together: four vertical panels sharing one x-axis — H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC, then a thin gene-model panel on the bottom. The gene track gets a height_ratios shrink and minimal styling (no y-ticks, no frame) so it reads as an annotation, not a fourth data series.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon

peaks = load_peaks(); genes = load_peak_genes()
x = peaks["position"]

# CREATE four panels — three signal, one gene model. gene panel is shortest.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    4, 1, figsize=(9.0, 5.0), sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 1, 1, 0.4], hspace=0.15))
ax_ac, ax_k4, ax_at, ax_g = axes

# three signal panels (same as step 3, each gets a colour + label)
for ax, col, color in [(ax_ac, "H3K27ac", RED),
                       (ax_k4, "H3K4me3", BLUE),
                       (ax_at, "ATAC",    GREEN)]:
    ax.fill_between(x, peaks[col], where=peaks[col] > 0, color=color, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_ylabel(col); ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# gene-model panel — minimal frame so it reads as annotation
def draw_gene(ax, row):
    y, h = 0, 0.5
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((row["start"], y - h / 2),
                           row["end"] - row["start"], h,
                           facecolor=PURPLE, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.8))
    if row["strand"] == "+":
        tip_x, base_x = row["end"], row["end"] - 400
    else:
        tip_x, base_x = row["start"], row["start"] + 400
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([(base_x, y - h / 2), (base_x, y + h / 2), (tip_x, y)],
                          facecolor=PURPLE, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.8))
    ax.text((row["start"] + row["end"]) / 2, y + 0.55, row["name"],
            ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")

for _, row in genes.iterrows():
    draw_gene(ax_g, row)
ax_g.set_ylim(-1, 1.4); ax_g.set_yticks([])               # no y-ticks on annotation
ax_g.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
ax_g.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

Peaks · Production Tool

Peaks · ecosystem

pyGenomeTracks for paper-grade multi-track plots

For real screenshots — dozens of tracks, BAM files, BigWig, BED, GTF, Hi-C — use pyGenomeTracks. You write a tiny .ini config and call one CLI command. It handles axes, scaling, gene model rendering, and Hi-C heatmaps that matplotlib can’t touch.

[H3K27ac]
file = H3K27ac.bw
title = H3K27ac
color = #B4405F
height = 1.5

[genes]
file = annotation.gtf
title = genes
style = UCSC
pyGenomeTracks --tracks tracks.ini --region chr2:1000-21000 -o figure.pdf

The matplotlib build you just saw is the mental model; pyGenomeTracks is the production tool.

Genome Stats · Takeaway

Genome stats · recap

Two stories, one principle

The bottom line 1. Coverage tells you what you can trust. A dumbbell sorted by loss surfaces the worst samples in one glance — bar charts of raw vs callable bury the story. 2. Peak tracks + gene models tell you what’s happening where. Stack one panel per signal, one panel for the gene model, all sharing the same x-axis. 3. The shared x-axis is the contract. Column-aligned positions across panels are what let the reader spot co-occurrence — without that, the panels are just three unrelated charts.

Circular Genome Plots

pyCirclize · Circos-style

Why Circular?

pyCirclize · theory

When the x-axis bends back on itself

Most genome views are linear: position on the x-axis, value on the y. That works for one chromosome at a time, and Manhattan plots cheat by laying 22 of them end-to-end. But the moment the relationships between chromosomes are the story — a translocation that moves a block from chr3 to chr14, a regulator on chr1 that drives expression on chr19, a Hi-C contact map — a line breaks.

Bend the axis into a circle and three things change:

  • Every chromosome becomes the same visual length to the eye, regardless of bp.
  • You can draw a chord between any two points without crossing the figure.
  • You can stack many concentric tracks (expression, methylation, density) without a vertical spaghetti of axes.

The trade-off: less detail within each chromosome (it’s a curved sliver), more visibility across them. Reach for circular when the answer is in the connections, not the local peaks.

Anatomy of a Circos Figure

pyCirclize · theory

Sectors, tracks, links — the three primitives

A circular plot has three building blocks:

  • Sectors — wedges of the ring, one per chromosome (or contig, or sample). The gap between them is a visual breath.
  • Tracks — concentric bands at radii (inner_r, outer_r). Each track holds one data layer: scatter, line, bar, heatmap.
  • Links — chords drawn through the centre, joining two genomic intervals on possibly different sectors.

Build a Circos by declaring the sectors first ({name: length}), then adding tracks to each sector and links between them.

Circos · The Data

pyCirclize · data peek

Same GWAS table, this time on a ring

load_gwas("height") is the table we already met for the Manhattan: one row per SNP, four columns. To draw it circular, we need one extra dictionary — the length of each chromosome — which is just max(pos) per chrom. That dictionary defines the sectors.

gwas = load_gwas("height")                # chrom, pos, pval, snp
gwas.head(5)
chrom pos pval snp
0 1 562879 0.197842 rs1217797
1 1 802716 0.454291 rs3152883
2 1 933561 0.750287 rs1966161
3 1 1294717 0.707315 rs2836508
4 1 1316327 0.553459 rs6514392 
# per-chromosome length = max position on that chromosome
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
{k: chrom_len[k] for k in list(chrom_len)[:4]}     # peek at first four
{1: 249795092, 2: 249744166, 3: 249840488, 4: 249737521}

Circos · Step 1 — Just the Sectors

pyCirclize · build

1 · The empty ring

Before any data, build the layout. The sectors dict maps chromosome name to length in bp; pyCirclize converts that into proportionally-sized wedges. We give each sector a label and draw — at this point the figure is a labelled empty ring, the canvas every other layer will rest on.

from pycirclize import Circos                     # the main class

gwas = load_gwas("height")                        # same table as Manhattan
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()

# sectors: {name: length_in_bp} — order = clockwise order on the ring
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                 # CREATE: 2deg gap between sectors

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)       # one label per chromosome
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)   # r = radius (axis is 0-100)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))          # CALL: returns matplotlib Figure

Circos · Step 2 — Axis & Ticks

pyCirclize · build

2 · Give each sector a measuring stick

A ring with no marks is pretty but useless — we can’t read positions. sector.axis() paints the outer boundary; sector.xticks_by_interval(...) drops tick marks at fixed bp intervals so the eye has anchors.

from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height")
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                          # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    # outer axis ring with line styling
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)
    # ticks live on a Track, not on the Sector itself — make a thin rim track at
    # the outer edge so the labels orbit the ring without overlapping data.
    rim = sector.add_track((96, 100))
    rim.xticks_by_interval(100_000_000,                                  # every 100 Mb
                           label_size=6, label_orientation="vertical",
                           label_formatter=lambda v: f"{v/1e6:.0f}M")    # bp -> Mb

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))                   # CALL

Circos · Step 3 — Manhattan-on-a-Ring

pyCirclize · build

3 · Skyscrapers, pointing outward

Add a scatter track at radii (60, 90) — a band between 60% and 90% of the ring. For each sector, pull just that chromosome’s SNPs out of the GWAS frame and scatter pos against -log10(p). Significance now points outward: the higher the dot, the closer to the sky.

from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])               # significance axis
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                       # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)

    # add a track at radii 60-90 (the band the SNP cloud lives in)
    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    # subset the dataframe to this chromosome only
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    # CALL: scatter SNP position vs -log10(p) inside the track
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                    # CALL

Circos · Step 4 — Hits & Threshold Ring

pyCirclize · build

4 · Colour what crossed the line

The same logic as the linear Manhattan: a dashed ring at -log10(5e-8), and the SNPs above it re-drawn in red on top of the grey cloud. The threshold becomes a circle; significance becomes everything that pokes through it.

from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}
gw_thresh = -np.log10(5e-8)                          # genome-wide significance

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                    # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)

    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    # background cloud — grey
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)
    # hits — significant SNPs re-drawn red, larger
    hits = df[df["pval"] < 5e-8]
    if not hits.empty:                                       # most chroms have no hits
        track.scatter(hits["pos"].to_numpy(), hits["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                      s=10, color=RED, alpha=0.95)
    # dashed threshold ring at y = -log10(5e-8)
    track.line([0, chrom_len[chrom_num]], [gw_thresh, gw_thresh],
               color=RED, lw=0.6, ls="--")

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                 # CALL

Circos · Step 5 — Chord Links

pyCirclize · build

5 · Connect the hits across chromosomes

The headline feature of any Circos plot: chords. circos.link((sector_a, start, end), (sector_b, start, end)) draws a quadratic Bezier through the centre joining two intervals. We use it here to connect the top-5 most significant SNPs to each other — real publications use the same primitive for translocations, synteny blocks, or cis-/trans-regulatory pairs.

from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}
gw_thresh = -np.log10(5e-8)

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                              # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)
    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)
    hits = df[df["pval"] < 5e-8]
    if not hits.empty:                                       # most chroms have no hits
        track.scatter(hits["pos"].to_numpy(), hits["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                      s=10, color=RED, alpha=0.95)
    track.line([0, chrom_len[chrom_num]], [gw_thresh, gw_thresh],
               color=RED, lw=0.6, ls="--")

# pick the top-5 strongest hits across the whole genome
top5 = gwas.nsmallest(5, "pval").reset_index(drop=True)

# draw a chord between consecutive pairs (1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5)
for i in range(len(top5) - 1):
    a, b = top5.iloc[i], top5.iloc[i + 1]
    if a["chrom"] == b["chrom"]:                               # skip intra-chrom
        continue
    # link: two (sector, start, end) tuples; +-1bp gives a thin chord
    circos.link((f"chr{a['chrom']}", int(a['pos']) - 1, int(a['pos']) + 1),
                (f"chr{b['chrom']}", int(b['pos']) - 1, int(b['pos']) + 1),
                color=PURPLE, alpha=0.55)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                           # CALL

Circos · Takeaway

pyCirclize · recap

Three primitives, any biology

The recipe 1. Sectors — {name: length} defines the ring; one wedge per chromosome. 2. Tracks — sector.add_track((inner_r, outer_r)) is a concentric data band; stack as many as the eye can read. 3. Links — circos.link(...) is a chord between two intervals; the answer to “which moved with which”.

Circular plots trade per-chromosome zoom for cross-chromosome reach. Use them when the story is relationships, not values — translocations, synteny, Hi-C contacts, regulator-target pairs. Same logic for bacterial genomes (one sector per replicon), for metagenomes (one sector per MAG), even for protein domains (one sector per chain).

Synteny Plots

Genome comparison · ribbons

What Is a Synteny Plot?

synteny · theory

Two genomes as tracks, ribbons as homology

A synteny plot stacks two (or more) chromosomes as horizontal tracks and connects matching regions with a ribbon. The geometry tells the story at a glance:

  • SYN — block in the same order on both genomes. The ribbon is a flat parallelogram. Conserved synteny is the uneventful answer.
  • INV — same region, opposite strand. The ribbon twists because we draw the bottom edge with its endpoints swapped. Inversions are common around centromeres and recombination cold spots.
  • TRANS — block at a different position on the other genome. The ribbon crosses or skews; the region is somewhere else now.

Reach for synteny when you have two assemblies and the question is structural: what stayed put, what flipped, what moved.

Today vs Day-1’s plotsr

synteny · positioning

Two complementary views of the same problem

On Day 1 we walked through plotsr: the CLI pipeline align -> SyRI -> plot, the genomes.txt, the *syri.out files, the configurable multi-genome figure. It is the production tool.

Today we drop one level lower. We will draw a synteny figure for two genomes in pure matplotlib, from Rectangle patches and Polygon ribbons. No SyRI, no plotsr — just primitives and a small DataFrame.

After this section, plotsr will feel like sugar: it is doing the same thing for N genomes that you are doing here for 2. Once you have built the ribbons yourself, you know which knob to turn when the published default does not fit your figure.

**Day 1 _15:** plotsr — production CLI, multi-genome, SyRI input. **Day 2 _07:** matplotlib — two genomes, ribbons from polygons, full control.

Synteny · Build the Toy Data

synteny · data

Six SYN blocks, one inversion, one translocation

We need a DataFrame with the homology calls. Each row is one block: where it lives on genome A, where it lives on genome B, and what type it is. The trick that encodes an inversion is dead simple — the B-coordinates are reversed (chrB_start > chrB_end), so when we later draw the polygon, the bottom edge twists.

# two "chromosomes", each 100 Mb in arbitrary units
LEN_A = 100.0
LEN_B = 100.0

# hand-built homology table: 6 SYN, 1 INV, 1 TRANS
blocks = pd.DataFrame([
    # SYN: A-coords and B-coords ascending, near-identical positions
    {"chrA_start":  5, "chrA_end": 18, "chrB_start":  6, "chrB_end": 19, "type": "SYN"},
    {"chrA_start": 22, "chrA_end": 30, "chrB_start": 23, "chrB_end": 31, "type": "SYN"},
    {"chrA_start": 34, "chrA_end": 45, "chrB_start": 35, "chrB_end": 46, "type": "SYN"},
    {"chrA_start": 58, "chrA_end": 68, "chrB_start": 59, "chrB_end": 69, "type": "SYN"},
    {"chrA_start": 72, "chrA_end": 80, "chrB_start": 73, "chrB_end": 81, "type": "SYN"},
    {"chrA_start": 92, "chrA_end": 98, "chrB_start": 93, "chrB_end": 99, "type": "SYN"},
    # INV: same span on A, but B-coords are reversed -> flipped strand
    {"chrA_start": 48, "chrA_end": 56, "chrB_start": 56, "chrB_end": 48, "type": "INV"},
    # TRANS: a block at A=82..90 lives at B=10..18 (somewhere else entirely)
    {"chrA_start": 82, "chrA_end": 90, "chrB_start": 10, "chrB_end": 18, "type": "TRANS"},
])
blocks.head(8)
chrA_start chrA_end chrB_start chrB_end type
0 5 18 6 19 SYN
1 22 30 23 31 SYN
2 34 45 35 46 SYN
3 58 68 59 69 SYN
4 72 80 73 81 SYN
5 92 98 93 99 SYN
6 48 56 56 48 INV
7 82 90 10 18 TRANS 
blocks["type"].value_counts()           # quick sanity check on the mix
type
SYN      6
INV      1
TRANS    1
Name: count, dtype: int64

Synteny · Step 1 — The Two Chromosomes

synteny · build

1 · Two rectangles, one above the other

Before any ribbons, place the two chromosomes. They are just Rectangle patches: bottom-left corner at (0, y), width = chromosome length, a thin height. Genome A goes on top, genome B on the bottom; the ribbons will eventually live in the gap between them.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle           # the chromosome bars

LEN_A, LEN_B = 100.0, 100.0                        # both 100 Mb units
Y_TOP, Y_BOT, BAR_H = 1.0, 0.0, 0.08               # y-positions and bar thickness

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))             # CREATE

# genome A — top bar
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_TOP), LEN_A, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=BLUE, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))    # CALL
# genome B — bottom bar
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_BOT), LEN_B, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=GREEN, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))   # CALL

# label each bar on the left
ax.text(-2, Y_TOP + BAR_H / 2, "Genome A",
        ha="right", va="center", fontsize=11, color=INK)
ax.text(-2, Y_BOT + BAR_H / 2, "Genome B",
        ha="right", va="center", fontsize=11, color=INK)

# cosmetic frame
ax.set_xlim(-10, max(LEN_A, LEN_B) + 5); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.5)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("position (Mb)")

Synteny · Step 2 — One Ribbon, By Hand

synteny · build

2 · A polygon with four vertices

A ribbon is a four-cornered polygon. The vertices go clockwise: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. Top edge sits on genome A; bottom edge sits on genome B. Pick the first SYN block and draw exactly one ribbon to feel the geometry.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon

LEN_A, LEN_B = 100.0, 100.0
Y_TOP, Y_BOT, BAR_H = 1.0, 0.0, 0.08

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))             # CREATE

ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_TOP), LEN_A, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=BLUE,  edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_BOT), LEN_B, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=GREEN, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))

# pick the first block: A=5..18, B=6..19, SYN
b = {"chrA_start": 5, "chrA_end": 18, "chrB_start": 6, "chrB_end": 19}

# vertex order — clockwise starting at top-left:
#   1. (A_start, top edge of B-A gap = Y_TOP)
#   2. (A_end,   top)
#   3. (B_end,   bottom edge = Y_BOT + BAR_H)
#   4. (B_start, bottom)
verts = [(b["chrA_start"], Y_TOP),                       # top-left
         (b["chrA_end"],   Y_TOP),                       # top-right
         (b["chrB_end"],   Y_BOT + BAR_H),               # bottom-right
         (b["chrB_start"], Y_BOT + BAR_H)]               # bottom-left
# CALL: filled polygon, low alpha so overlaps remain visible
ax.add_patch(Polygon(verts, closed=True,
                     facecolor=GREY, edgecolor="none", alpha=0.45))

ax.text(-2, Y_TOP + BAR_H / 2, "Genome A", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.text(-2, Y_BOT + BAR_H / 2, "Genome B", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(-10, max(LEN_A, LEN_B) + 5); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.5)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("position (Mb)")

Synteny · Step 3 — All Blocks, Coloured by Type

synteny · build

3 · The canonical figure

Now sweep through the whole DataFrame. The polygon shape is identical for every block — vertex order top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left — but the meaning changes with type:

  • For SYN (grey), chrB_start < chrB_end, so the bottom edge goes left-to-right, same as the top — a flat parallelogram.
  • For INV (amber), chrB_start > chrB_end, so the bottom edge reverses, creating a visual twist.
  • For TRANS (blue), the B-coordinates live somewhere unrelated to the A-coordinates, so the ribbon skews across the figure.
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon

# colour map — one fill per block type
TYPE_COLOUR = {"SYN": GREY, "INV": AMBER, "TRANS": BLUE}

LEN_A, LEN_B = 100.0, 100.0
Y_TOP, Y_BOT, BAR_H = 1.0, 0.0, 0.08

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))                # CREATE

ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_TOP), LEN_A, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=BLUE,  edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_BOT), LEN_B, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=GREEN, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))

# one polygon per row of the blocks DataFrame — vectorise via itertuples
for b in blocks.itertuples(index=False):
    verts = [(b.chrA_start, Y_TOP),                   # top-left
             (b.chrA_end,   Y_TOP),                   # top-right
             (b.chrB_end,   Y_BOT + BAR_H),           # bottom-right
             (b.chrB_start, Y_BOT + BAR_H)]           # bottom-left
    # INV: chrB_start > chrB_end -> bottom edge reverses -> visual twist
    # TRANS: B-coords far from A-coords -> ribbon skews
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(verts, closed=True,
                         facecolor=TYPE_COLOUR[b.type],
                         edgecolor="none", alpha=0.55))   # CALL

ax.text(-2, Y_TOP + BAR_H / 2, "Genome A", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.text(-2, Y_BOT + BAR_H / 2, "Genome B", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(-10, max(LEN_A, LEN_B) + 5); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.5)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("position (Mb)")

Synteny · Step 4 — Legend, Ticks, Title

synteny · build

4 · Polish — orient the reader

The figure is informative but spare. Add a tick every 20 Mb so the eye can read positions, a legend mapping colour to block type, and a title that names what we are looking at.

from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon

TYPE_COLOUR = {"SYN": GREY, "INV": AMBER, "TRANS": BLUE}
LEN_A, LEN_B = 100.0, 100.0
Y_TOP, Y_BOT, BAR_H = 1.0, 0.0, 0.08

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))               # CREATE

ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_TOP), LEN_A, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=BLUE,  edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, Y_BOT), LEN_B, BAR_H,
                       facecolor=GREEN, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.6))

for b in blocks.itertuples(index=False):
    verts = [(b.chrA_start, Y_TOP),
             (b.chrA_end,   Y_TOP),
             (b.chrB_end,   Y_BOT + BAR_H),
             (b.chrB_start, Y_BOT + BAR_H)]
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(verts, closed=True,
                         facecolor=TYPE_COLOUR[b.type],
                         edgecolor="none", alpha=0.55))

ax.text(-2, Y_TOP + BAR_H / 2, "Genome A", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.text(-2, Y_BOT + BAR_H / 2, "Genome B", ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(-10, max(LEN_A, LEN_B) + 5); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.7)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

# orientation ticks every 20 Mb
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, 101, 20))
ax.set_xlabel("position (Mb)")

# legend — one Patch handle per block type
legend_handles = [mpatches.Patch(facecolor=TYPE_COLOUR[t], alpha=0.55, label=t)
                  for t in ["SYN", "INV", "TRANS"]]
ax.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="upper right",
          frameon=False, fontsize=9, ncol=3,
          bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.18))

# narrative title — the figure has a point
ax.set_title("Genome A vs Genome B - 6 syntenic blocks, 1 inversion, 1 translocation",
             loc="left", fontsize=11, color=INK, pad=14)

Synteny · Takeaway

synteny · recap

The whole figure is one Polygon call in a loop

The recipe 1. Two Rectangle bars — one per genome, parallel and labelled. 2. One Polygon per block, four vertices in clockwise order. Top edge on A, bottom edge on B. 3. Vertex order encodes the rearrangement. Bottom edge reversed = inversion; bottom edge far from top = translocation. 4. Colour encodes the type. Grey for conserved, amber for flipped, blue for moved.

Once you can draw this in matplotlib, packages like plotsr (Day 1) and pyCirclize feel like syntactic sugar over the same idea — they stack the bars, parse the homology table, and draw the polygons for you. Knowing the primitive means you can debug or customise any of them when the default does not say what your figure needs to say.
